bug_description.normalized:
The staged 114-byte witness is copied into lwan's static `data_copy` request buffer and binds `helper->buffer->len = 114` with `helper->header_start` pointing at the fixed global array `header_start[64]`. The witness bytes are `GET / HTTP/1.1`, then 31 repetitions of `"  "`, then `

 `. `read_request_finalizer()` admits the buffer because it finds `

` at offsets 108..111, `identify_http_path()` accepts `GET / HTTP/1.1`, and `parse_headers()` begins scanning the malformed tail. Each non-empty header consumes two `header_start` slots (`start` and `end`), so after 32 iterations the loop has filled `header_start[0..63]` and advanced to the final `" "` fragment with `n_headers == 64`. The vulnerable post-store guard `if (n_headers > N_HEADER_START || p >= buffer_end)` does not reject this exact-full state because `N_HEADER_START` is 64 and the first disjunct uses `>` instead of `>=`. On the next iteration `header_start[n_headers++] = next_chr` writes index 64, an 8-byte store immediately past the 64-element global array. AddressSanitizer reports the resulting global-buffer-overflow WRITE in `parse_headers`, with stack `parse_headers -> parse_http_request -> fuzz_parse_http_request`.

source.description: The fuzz target first materializes the attacker-controlled bytes into the exact static request buffer whose malformed layout later drives `parse_headers()` past `header_start[64]`.
source.value_from: The staged witness file `gt_results/arvo_14529/poc` (sha256 `576624e3a49fedc37df80a208ce4b9b7188c55d341af9d9f8d9a71633e8566af`) is 114 bytes long. It begins with `GET / HTTP/1.1\r`, then contains 31 repetitions of `"  \r"`, then ends with `\r\n\r\n \r`.

root_cause.code: if (n_headers > N_HEADER_START || p >= buffer_end) { helper->n_header_start = 0; return false; }
root_cause.description: The only bounds check for `header_start` runs after both stores and uses `n_headers > N_HEADER_START` instead of `>=`. When the witness makes `n_headers == 64`, the full 64-slot array is treated as safe and the loop continues into one more write.
root_cause.note: The fixing commit changes this predicate to `n_headers >= N_HEADER_START`, preventing the exact-full boundary from reaching the next pair of stores.

sink.description: ASan sink. On the 33rd non-empty header fragment, the first pair-store writes `header_start[64]`, one pointer past the 64-element global array `header_start`.
sink.note: The sanitizer trace reports `AddressSanitizer: global-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8` at `parse_headers` line 553 and says the faulting address is 0 bytes to the right of global variable `header_start` defined at `lwan-request.c:1653` with size 512.

tainted_value_origin.description: This helper binds the copied attacker bytes to the parser extent `len = 114` and to the fixed destination array `header_start[64]`; `parse_headers()` later derives `buffer_end` from that tainted length while reusing the same `header_start` pointer for every start/end store.

parser_admitted.description: The saved witness contains `\r\n\r\n` at offsets 108..111, so `has_crlfcrlf()` succeeds and `read_request_finalizer()` returns `FINALIZER_DONE`. `fuzz_parse_http_request()` therefore reaches `parse_http_request()`, and the saved ASan stack confirms the admitted path is `parse_headers -> parse_http_request -> fuzz_parse_http_request`.

coarse_trace.summary: The staged 114-byte witness is copied into static `data_copy`, exposed to the parser as `helper.buffer` with `len = 114`, and admitted by `read_request_finalizer()` because the buffer contains `\r\n\r\n`.
The request line `GET / HTTP/1.1` is accepted, `identify_http_path()` returns the malformed header tail, and `parse_http_request()` invokes `parse_headers()` on that tail.

The header scan records 32 prior start/end pointer pairs into `header_start[0..63]`, leaving `n_headers == 64`, but the vulnerable `n_headers > N_HEADER_START` check does not reject the exact-full boundary.
The next malformed fragment is still treated as a non-empty header, and the first pair-store writes `header_start[64]`, producing the ASan global-buffer-overflow write.

fine_trace.note: The saved 114-byte witness is copied verbatim into the static global request buffer `data_copy`. Its structure is `GET / HTTP/1.1\r`, then 31 repetitions of `"  \r"`, then `\r\n\r\n \r`.

The parser helper now aliases the attacker bytes as a 114-byte request buffer and points header parsing at the fixed global array `header_start[N_HEADER_START]`. In this build `N_HEADER_START` is 64, so the destination capacity is exactly 64 pointers / 512 bytes.

By the time `parse_headers()` runs, `identify_http_path()` has accepted `GET / HTTP/1.1` and returned the byte after the request-line CR. This setup makes `buffer_end = data_copy + 114`, aliases the same 64-slot `header_start` array from step 2, initializes `n_headers = 0`, and starts the scan at byte 16 of the malformed tail (`p = buffer + 1`).

On the saved witness, this pair-store/advance block executes 32 times before the crashing iteration. The malformed tail yields 32 prior non-empty fragments, so these safe iterations fill `header_start[0..63]`, leave `n_headers == 64`, and advance `p` to `data_copy + 112`, the final `" \r"` fragment.

Root cause. At the exact-full boundary reached in step 4, `n_headers == 64` and `p == data_copy + 112 < buffer_end`, so this guard evaluates false: `64 > 64` is false and the end-of-buffer check is also false. Because the check runs after the pair-store block and uses `>` instead of `>=`, the full array is not rejected before the next write.

Because step 5 let the loop continue with `p = data_copy + 112`, the next iteration materializes `next_chr = data_copy + 112` and `next_hdr = data_copy + 113` from the witness's final `" \r"` bytes. `next_chr != next_hdr`, so the blank-line termination path is not taken and control falls through to the pair-store block again.

ASan sink. `n_headers` is still 64 from step 4, so this first store of the 33rd pair targets `header_start[64]`. `header_start` was declared as `static char *header_start[N_HEADER_START];` with `N_HEADER_START == 64`, so index 64 is one element past the 512-byte global array. AddressSanitizer reports the resulting 8-byte global-buffer-overflow write at this line.

allocation_context.note: ASan reports the invalid write is 0 bytes to the right of global variable `header_start` defined here with size 512.

crash_stack.function: fuzzer::FuzzerDriver(int*, char***, int (*)(unsigned char const*, unsigned long))

poc.trigger: Stage 01 reproduced the vulnerable crash by running `PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_14529 run --version vulnerable --expect crash`, which fed the saved witness file `poc` to `/out/request_fuzzer` and produced `AddressSanitizer: global-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8 in parse_headers`.

format.name: HTTP request bytes parsed by lwan request_fuzzer
format.contract: The saved witness is exactly 114 bytes: `GET / HTTP/1.1\r`, then 31 repetitions of `"  \r"`, then `\r\n\r\n \r`. In this exact layout, `parse_headers()` reaches `n_headers == 64` after 32 non-empty fragments, the vulnerable `n_headers > N_HEADER_START` guard fails open at that exact-full boundary, and the next fragment `" \r"` forces the out-of-bounds write to `header_start[64]`.
